questions.q: Why does an open redirect help bypass SSRF URL filters?
o: Open redirects encrypt the internal URL so the filter cannot inspect it
The filter checks only the initial URL, which can point to an allowed external path, while the server follows a redirect to the blocked internal destination
Open redirects disable the server's HTTP client entirely
Open redirects require the attacker to authenticate first
questions.x: The SSRF filter validates the stockApi or similar parameter before the request is made. If that value points to an allowed on-domain redirect endpoint, the filter passes it. The server then follows the redirect to an internal address the filter would have blocked directly.
questions.h: The filter sees the first URL. What happens after the server follows a redirect to an internal target?

questions.q: In the SSRF + open redirect chain, why does the initial URL appear safe to the filter?
o: It uses HTTPS which all filters allow
It points to the same domain or a relative path on the victim site, which passes same-origin or allowlist checks
It encodes the internal IP in base64
It uses a DNS rebinding technique
questions.x: Filters often allow URLs that start with / or belong to the application's own domain. Pointing stockApi at /product/nextProduct?path=... looks like a normal internal request rather than a direct internal IP address.
questions.h: The filter is checking whether the submitted URL looks external or internal. What does a same-domain redirect endpoint look like to that check?

questions.q: What role does the open redirection endpoint play in the exploit chain?
o: It makes the SSRF request from the attacker's browser
It acts as a proxy that redirects the server's outbound request to the internal target the filter blocked
It stores the internal admin credentials for later use
It encrypts the SSRF payload before transmission
questions.x: The open redirect endpoint accepts a user-controlled destination and issues a 302 redirect. When the server's HTTP client follows that redirect, it reaches the internal admin interface without the filter ever inspecting the final URL.
questions.h: The redirect endpoint does not fetch the internal URL itself for the attacker. It tells the server's HTTP client where to go next.

questions.q: Why is checking only the initial URL insufficient when the HTTP client follows redirects?
o: Redirects always fail on HTTPS connections
The HTTP client may automatically follow 3xx redirects to a different host or IP that the initial URL filter never evaluated
Redirects strip authentication headers from the request
Redirects only work for GET requests to public APIs
questions.x: Most server-side HTTP libraries follow redirects by default. The filter sees https://victim.com/redirect?url=... and allows it, but the client ends up at http://192.168.x.x/admin after following the redirect chain.
questions.h: Think about what happens after the server receives a 302 response pointing to an internal IP. Does the filter get a second chance to inspect that destination?

questions.q: What is the most thorough fix for SSRF bypass via open redirects?
o: Block all HTTP redirects globally
Validate the initial URL and also validate redirect destinations against the same allowlist at the HTTP client level
Require authentication on every internal admin panel
Remove all redirect endpoints from the application
questions.x: Fixing only the initial URL is not enough when redirects are followed automatically. The HTTP client must reject any redirect that leads to a private IP range, localhost, or other blocked destination.
questions.h: There are two points where the server could catch this: the initial URL and the redirect destination. Which fix addresses both?
